<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwCg"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rayleigh_sunlight_scattering.png" class="mw-file-description" id="mwCw"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rayleigh_sunlight_scattering.png" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Rayleigh_sunlight_scattering.png/500px-Rayleigh_sunlight_scattering.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/69/Rayleigh_sunlight_scattering.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled 2x" data-file-width="600" data-file-height="491" data-file-type="bitmap" height="393" width="480" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.9" id="mwDA"></a><figcaption id="mwDQ">In <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere" title="Earth's atmosphere" class="mw-redirect" id="mwDg">Earth's atmosphere</a>, the dominant scattering efficiency of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_blue" title="Sky blue" id="mwDw">blue light</a> is compared to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_spectrum#Spectral_colors" title="Visible spectrum" id="mwEA">red or green</a> light. Scattering and absorption are major causes of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attenuation" title="Attenuation" id="mwEQ">attenuation</a> of sunlight radiation by the atmosphere. During broad <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight" title="Daylight" id="mwEg">daylight</a>, the sky is blue due to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_scattering" title="Rayleigh scattering" id="mwEw">Rayleigh scattering</a>, while around sunrise or sunset, and especially during <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight" title="Twilight" id="mwFA">twilight</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappuis_absorption" title="Chappuis absorption" id="mwFQ">absorption</a> of irradiation by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone#Spectroscopic_properties" title="Ozone" id="mwFg">ozone</a> helps maintain blue color in the evening sky. At sunrise or sunset, tangentially incident solar rays illuminate clouds with orange to red hues.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwFw"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spectrum_of_blue_sky.svg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwGA"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spectrum_of_blue_sky.svg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Spectrum_of_blue_sky.svg/500px-Spectrum_of_blue_sky.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Spectrum_of_blue_sky.svg/960px-Spectrum_of_blue_sky.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="2531" data-file-height="1600" data-file-type="drawing" height="303" width="480" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.9" id="mwGQ"></a><figcaption id="mwGg">The visible spectrum, approximately 380 to 740 nanometers (nm),<sup about="#mwt8" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-1"}}"><a href="#cite_note-1" id="mwGw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwHA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwHQ">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwHg">]</span></span></a></sup> shows the atmospheric water absorption band and the solar <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraunhofer_lines" title="Fraunhofer lines" id="mwHw">Fraunhofer lines</a>. The blue sky spectrum contains light at all visible wavelengths with a broad maximum around 450–485 nm, the wavelengths of the color blue.</figcaption></figure>

<p id="mwIA"><b id="mwIQ">Diffuse sky radiation</b>, is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_radiation" title="Solar radiation" class="mw-redirect" id="mwIg">solar radiation</a> reaching the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth" title="Earth" id="mwIw">Earth</a>'s surface after having been <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scattering" title="Scattering" id="mwJA">scattered</a> from the direct solar beam by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecule" title="Molecule" id="mwJQ">molecules</a> or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particulates" title="Particulates" class="mw-redirect" id="mwJg">particulates</a> in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere" title="Earth's atmosphere" class="mw-redirect" id="mwJw">atmosphere</a>. It is also called <b id="mwKA">sky radiation</b>,  the determinative process for changing the colors of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky" title="Sky" id="mwKQ">sky</a>. It is normally measured on a horizontal surface, thus frequently termed <b id="mwKg">diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI)</b>, often in the unit of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt" title="Watt" id="mwKw">watts</a> per square meter (W/m<sup id="mwLA">2</sup>). Approximately 23% of direct incident radiation of total <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mwLQ">sunlight</a> is removed from the direct solar beam by scattering into the atmosphere; of this amount (of incident radiation)  about two-thirds ultimately reaches the earth as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photon_diffusion" title="Photon diffusion" id="mwLg">photon diffused</a> skylight radiation.<link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:All_articles_with_unsourced_statements" about="#mwt9" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwLw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"citation needed","href":"./Template:Citation_needed"},"params":{"date":{"wt":"March 2016"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_with_unsourced_statements_from_March_2016" about="#mwt9"><sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;" about="#mwt9" id="mwMA"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span><i><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2016)">citation needed</span></a></i><span typeof="mw:Entity">]</span></sup></p>

<p id="mwMQ">The dominant radiative scattering processes in the atmosphere are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_scattering" title="Rayleigh scattering" id="mwMg">Rayleigh scattering</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_scattering" title="Mie scattering" id="mwMw">Mie scattering</a>; they are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elastic_scattering" title="Elastic scattering" id="mwNA">elastic</a>, meaning that a photon of light can be deviated from its path without being absorbed and without changing wavelength.</p>

<p id="mwNQ">Under an overcast sky, there is no direct sunlight, and all light results from diffused skylight radiation.</p>

<p id="mwNg">Proceeding from analyses of the aftermath of the eruption of the Philippines volcano Mount Pinatubo (in June 1991) and other studies:<sup about="#mwt10" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-web.archive.org_2-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"web.archive.org"}}"><a href="#cite_note-web.archive.org-2" id="mwNw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwOA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwOQ">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwOg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt13" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-3"}}"><a href="#cite_note-3" id="mwOw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwPA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwPQ">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwPg">]</span></span></a></sup>  Diffused skylight, owing to its intrinsic structure and behavior, can illuminate under-canopy leaves, permitting more efficient total whole-plant photosynthesis than would otherwise be the case; this in stark contrast to the effect of totally clear skies with direct sunlight that casts shadows onto understory leaves and thereby limits plant photosynthesis to the top canopy layer, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="#The_diffused_skylight_effect" class="mw-selflink-fragment" id="mwPw">(see below)</a>.</p>

<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" id="mwQA" data-mw="{"autoGenerated":true}"></section><section data-mw-section-id="1" id="mwQQ" aria-labelledby="Color"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Color">Color</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Diffuse_sky_radiation&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Color"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwQg"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trees-sky.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwQw"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trees-sky.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Trees-sky.jpg/500px-Trees-sky.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Trees-sky.jpg/960px-Trees-sky.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="1003" data-file-height="670" data-file-type="bitmap" height="254" width="380" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.5" id="mwRA"></a><figcaption id="mwRQ">A clear daytime sky, looking toward the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenith" title="Zenith" id="mwRg">zenith</a></figcaption></figure>

<p id="mwRw"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth" title="Atmosphere of Earth" id="mwSA">Earth's atmosphere</a> scatters short-<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength" title="Wavelength" id="mwSQ">wavelength</a> light more efficiently than that of longer wavelengths. Because its wavelengths are shorter,  blue light is more strongly scattered than the longer-wavelength lights, red or green. Hence, the result that when looking at the sky away from the direct incident <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mwSg">sunlight</a>, the human perceives the sky to be blue.<sup about="#mwt15" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-4" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-4"}}"><a href="#cite_note-4" id="mwSw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwTA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwTQ">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwTg">]</span></span></a></sup> The color perceived is similar to that presented by a monochromatic blue (at wavelength <span class="nowrap" about="#mwt14" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwTw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"nobr","href":"./Template:Nobr"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"474–476 [[Nanometer|nm]]"}},"i":0}}]}">474–476 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanometer" title="Nanometer" class="mw-redirect">nm</a></span>) mixed with white light, that is, an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_(color_theory)" title="Saturation (color theory)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwUA">unsaturated</a> blue light.<sup about="#mwt18" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-5" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-5"}}"><a href="#cite_note-5" id="mwUQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwUg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwUw">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwVA">]</span></span></a></sup> The explanation of blue color by  <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_William_Strutt,_3rd_Baron_Rayleigh" title="John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh" id="mwVQ">Lord Rayleigh</a> in 1871 is a famous example of applying <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimensional_analysis" title="Dimensional analysis" id="mwVg">dimensional analysis</a> to solving problems in physics.<sup about="#mwt21" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-6" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-6"}}"><a href="#cite_note-6" id="mwVw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwWA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWQ">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwWw">Scattering and absorption are major causes of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attenuation" title="Attenuation" id="mwXA">attenuation</a> of sunlight radiation by the atmosphere. Scattering varies as a function of the ratio of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_size" title="Particle size" id="mwXQ">particle diameters</a> (of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particulates" title="Particulates" class="mw-redirect" id="mwXg">particulates</a> in the atmosphere) to the wavelength of the incident radiation. When this ratio is less than about one-tenth, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_scattering" title="Rayleigh scattering" id="mwXw">Rayleigh scattering</a> occurs. (In this case, the scattering coefficient varies inversely with the fourth power of the wavelength. At larger ratios scattering varies in a more complex fashion, as described for spherical particles by the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_scattering" title="Mie scattering" id="mwYA">Mie theory</a>.) The laws of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_optics" title="Geometric optics" class="mw-redirect" id="mwYQ">geometric optics</a> begin to apply at higher ratios.</p>

<p id="mwYg">Daily at any global venue experiencing <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunrise" title="Sunrise" id="mwYw">sunrise</a> or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset" title="Sunset" id="mwZA">sunset</a>, most of the solar beam of visible sunlight arrives nearly <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_lines_to_circles" title="Tangent lines to circles" id="mwZQ">tangentially</a> to Earth's surface. Here, the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_path" title="Optical path" id="mwZg">path</a> of sunlight <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_mass_(astronomy)" title="Air mass (astronomy)" id="mwZw">through the atmosphere</a> is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_path_length" title="Optical path length" id="mwaA">elongated</a> such that much of the blue or green light is scattered away from the line of perceivable visible light. This phenomenon leaves the Sun's rays, and the clouds they illuminate, abundantly orange-to-red in colors, which one sees when looking at a sunset or sunrise.</p>

<p id="mwaQ">For the example of the Sun at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenith" title="Zenith" id="mwag">zenith</a>, in broad daylight, the sky is blue due to Rayleigh scattering, which also involves the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatomic" title="Diatomic" class="mw-redirect" id="mwaw">diatomic</a> gases <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen" title="Nitrogen" id="mwbA"><span class="chemf nowrap" about="#mwt23" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwbQ" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"chem","href":"./Template:Chem"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"N"},"2":{"wt":"2"}},"i":0}}]}">N<span class="nowrap"><span style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><sup style="font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline"></sup><br><sub style="font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline">2</sub></span></span></span></a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen" title="Oxygen" id="mwbg"><span class="chemf nowrap" about="#mwt24" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwbw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"chem","href":"./Template:Chem"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"O"},"2":{"wt":"2"}},"i":0}}]}">O<span class="nowrap"><span style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><sup style="font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline"></sup><br><sub style="font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline">2</sub></span></span></span></a>. Near sunset and especially during <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight" title="Twilight" id="mwcA">twilight</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappuis_absorption" title="Chappuis absorption" id="mwcQ">absorption</a> by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone" title="Ozone" id="mwcg">ozone</a> (<span class="chemf nowrap" about="#mwt22" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwcw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"chem","href":"./Template:Chem"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"O"},"2":{"wt":"3"}},"i":0}}]}">O<span class="nowrap"><span style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><sup style="font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline"></sup><br><sub style="font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline">3</sub></span></span></span>) significantly contributes to maintaining <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_hour" title="Blue hour" id="mwdA">blue color</a> in the evening sky.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="2" id="mwdQ" aria-labelledby="Under_an_overcast_sky"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Under_an_overcast_sky">Under an overcast sky</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Diffuse_sky_radiation&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Under an overcast sky"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwdg">There is essentially no direct sunlight under an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overcast" title="Overcast" id="mwdw">overcast</a> sky, so all light is then diffuse sky radiation. The flux of light is not very wavelength-dependent because the cloud droplets are larger than the light's wavelength and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_scattering" title="Mie scattering" id="mweA">scatter all colors</a> approximately equally. The light passes through the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_and_translucency" title="Transparency and translucency" id="mweQ">translucent</a> clouds in a manner similar to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frosted_glass" title="Frosted glass" id="mweg">frosted glass</a>. The intensity ranges (roughly) from <style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1154941027" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt25" id="mwew" <section data-mw-section-id="6" id="mwAUA" aria-labelledby="The_diffused_skylight_effect"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="The_diffused_skylight_effect">The diffused skylight effect</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Diffuse_sky_radiation&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: The diffused skylight effect"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAUE"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Canopy.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAUI"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Canopy.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Canopy.jpg/250px-Canopy.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Canopy.jpg/500px-Canopy.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="600" data-file-type="bitmap" height="188" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAUM"></a><figcaption id="mwAUQ">Well lit understorey areas due to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overcast" title="Overcast" id="mwAUU">overcast</a> clouds creating diffuse/<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_light" title="Soft light" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAUY">soft sunlight</a> conditions, that permits photosynthesis on leaves under the canopy.</figcaption></figure> 
<p id="mwAUc">This diffused skylight, owing to its intrinsic nature, can illuminate under-<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canopy_(biology)" title="Canopy (biology)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAUg">canopy</a> leaves permitting more efficient total whole-plant <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis" title="Photosynthesis" id="mwAUk">photosynthesis</a> than would otherwise be the case,<sup about="#mwt90" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-web.archive.org_2-5" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref"
